system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2198-05-05 23:10:00 to 2198-05-10 12:30:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 30-year-old woman with Type 1 diabetes and a history of gastroparesis was admitted for intractable nausea and vomiting, unable to tolerate oral intake. She was managed with IV fluids, antiemetics including Reglan as a substitute for non-formulary domperidone, and insulin therapy with D5W to address urinary ketones. Her hypertension was controlled with IV metoprolol initially, then transitioned to oral medications. She gradually advanced her diet, tolerating a full meal by discharge. A chest X-ray showed no new abnormalities, and urine culture indicated contamination without infection. Porphyria testing was negative, though pheochromocytoma evaluation was incomplete due to non-compliance with urine collection. She was discharged home on her prior medications with follow-up scheduled with her GI physician.
problems: Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type I [juvenile type], uncontrolled

Brief Hospital Course:
___ y/o female with DM1, numerous admissions for gastroparesis, 
nausea, vomiting who was admitted with diabetic ketoacidosis.
.
# Diabetic Ketoacidosis due to gastroparesis: in setting of 
anion gap acidosis (AG 28) with moderate acetone and ___ > 400; 
all consistent with DKA in setting of gastroparesis and 
longstanding IDDM. Unclear etiology for current flair. Was 
placed on an insulin drip until her anion gap closed on ___. 
She was then continued on an insulin gtt for an additional 24 
hours given poor oral intake. With continued controlled blood 
sugar with SC insulin, she was transitioned off the infusion and 
continued on a subcutaneous sliding scale per ___ 
recommendations. No etiology beyond a known history of 
gastroparesis was found for her current presentation. Infectious 
work-up was negative. On discharge, patient's blood sugars were 
well controlled with lantus 28 units at supper-time, and RISS. 
Gastroenterology followed the patient throughout her stay. There 
was consideration for EGD with Botox injections, but this will 
be pursued as an outpatient with her GI physician ___.
.
# Anion gap acidosis: likely related to DKA, lactate elevated to 
3.7 on admission. She took her full dose lantus night prior to 
admission, no insulin the day of admission given nausea. As 
above, gap closed with insulin infusion. Potassium was monitored 
closely and repleated as needed and lactic acidosis resolved to 
1.0 on discharge.  
.
# Nausea/vomiting: consistent with DKA in setting of 
gastroparesis and longstanding DM. Unclear etiology for current 
flair. LFTs and lipase wnl. Denies non-compliance. Has not 
tolerated erythromycin in the past for her gastroparesis. Was 
continued on home anti-emetics. Also, during this admission, 
there was witnessed induction of vomiting and concern for 
intentional coughing triggering post-tussive emesis for which 
patient met with SW (see below).
.
# Hypertension: Poorly controlled upon arrival. Patient states 
she takes lisinopril but not metoprolol (though on prior d/c 
summary). Given initial NPO status, was continued on enalapril 
and metoprolol IV. Once she was tolerating PO foods, these were 
converted to her home blood pressure regimen with good control.
.
# Urinary retention: Patient stated she had no urge to urinate 
the day of admission but foley was placed with 900cc urine 
output. Denies any fever, chills or preceeding dysuria. No 
changes in lower extremity strength, numbness or saddle 
sensation. Urinalysis was not indicative of infection.  Foley 
was removed the within 48 hours and she had no evidence of 
retention.
.  
# Diabetes Mellitus: As above, was controlled initially with 
insulin infusion, and then transitioned to subcutaneous dosing. 
On discharge, she was placed on her same regimen prior to 
admission with good blood sugar control. This discharge regimen 
was 28 units lantus with supper and RISS.
.
# Social: numerous admissions for gastroparesis/DKA. Has seen 
psych in the past as well. Also, during this admission, there 
was witnessed induction of vomiting and concern for intentional 
coughing triggering post-tussive emesis. Met with SW; 
consideration for domestic violence screen given repeated 
hospitalizations with concern for secondary gain. However, per 
SW impression, there was no concern for domestic violence or 
secondary gain.
.
# Dispo: discharge to home, PCP and GI ___, consideration 
for outpatient EGD with botox injection

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi… I’ve been so nauseous all day. Started around 5 a.m. Then in the evening, I started vomiting nonstop and was sweating a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any pain with it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, a little on the right side of my belly, but not too bad. Mostly just the nausea and throwing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We checked your blood sugar when you came in—it was very high, 529. And we found ketones, which means you were in diabetic ketoacidosis, or DKA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… that’s why I feel so awful. I took my Lantus the night before, but I couldn’t keep anything down today, so I didn’t take any insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Because of the DKA, you were transferred to the ICU for an insulin IV to bring your levels down safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right… I remember getting that. My stomach’s been so bad for so long. Is it just my gastroparesis flaring again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely the main trigger. Your labs showed an anion gap of 28, which confirms DKA, and your lactate was high too, at 3.7. But we’re treating that with insulin and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure was really high too, wasn’t it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was up to the 180s. You said you take lisinopril but not metoprolol anymore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I stopped metoprolol because it made me tired. But I still take lisinopril.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Since you couldn’t eat at first, we gave you IV medications to control your blood pressure. Once you can eat, we’ll switch back to your usual pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. I also couldn’t pee all day… that’s why they put in a catheter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you had about 900 mL in your bladder. But no signs of infection, and you’ve been able to go on your own since then. We removed the catheter yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your anion gap has closed—down to 11 now—and your blood sugar is much better. The insulin drip is being stopped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Does that mean I’m out of the woods?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The DKA is resolved, yes. But your nausea and vomiting are still ongoing. We’re continuing your usual anti-nausea meds—domperidone, Zofran, and Compazine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve tried so many things… erythromycin made me worse before. Is there anything else we can do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The GI team is following you. They’ve suggested an outpatient EGD with possible Botox injections into your stomach to help with the gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve heard about that. Would that really help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can help some patients reduce nausea and vomiting. It’s not permanent, but it might give you relief for a few months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d like to try it, if my GI doctor thinks it’s right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed something—we saw you putting your finger in your throat and coughing hard before vomiting. Can you tell me about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I… sometimes I feel like I need to get it over with. The nausea is so bad, I just want to vomit and be done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand it’s distressing. A social worker spoke with you yesterday—was that helpful?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, she was kind. I just feel stuck in this cycle. Every time I get sick, I end up here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to support you. The good news is your labs are improving. Your lactate is down to 1.0, and your kidneys are fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re starting to advance your diet—clear liquids first, then soft foods if you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous… I haven’t kept anything down in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go slow. Small sips. And we’ll keep your anti-nausea meds going around the clock for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor? I had some apple juice and crackers… and I kept them down!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent! That’s a big step forward. Let’s try a soft meal later and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. You’ve been tolerating regular food, your blood sugars are stable on subcutaneous insulin, and your vitals are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I might be able to go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow or the day after. We’ll make sure you’re steady on your feet and managing meals first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on the same insulin as before—28 units Lantus at supper, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And Humalog as needed with meals, based on your blood sugar. We’ll send that home with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure meds—lisinopril and metoprolol—both again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your pressure has been well-controlled since switching back to oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last night’s blood sugar was 98, and your morning labs look great. You’re on track for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s such a relief. What about the EGD with Botox?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll set up a referral to your GI doctor. They’ll decide if it’s right for you and schedule it as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I start vomiting again at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep using your anti-nausea meds as prescribed. If you can’t keep fluids down, or your blood sugar goes very high, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll have your discharge papers ready soon. You’re going home with the same meds, no changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up with my GI doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll schedule that. And your primary care doctor too. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just wanted to say thanks again. I feel so much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad to hear that. Keep up with your insulin and diet, and take your anti-nausea meds as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been writing down my blood sugars. Is that helpful?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. It helps you and your doctors see patterns. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re cleared to go home. Rest, stay hydrated, and follow up with your GI doctor about the EGD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I wear my scopolamine patch?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue it every 72 hours as before. It may help with nausea, especially if you’re traveling or feeling unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m just glad to be feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad too. Take it easy and keep in touch with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve packed up. Ready when you are.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Discharge papers are signed. You’re officially going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I’ll follow up with my doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Take care of yourself.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 30-year-old woman with Type 1 diabetes and a history of gastroparesis was admitted for diabetic ketoacidosis triggered by severe nausea and vomiting. She presented with high blood glucose, an anion gap of 28, and ketonuria, requiring ICU-level care and an insulin infusion. Her DKA resolved within 24 hours, but nausea persisted. She was managed with IV fluids, antiemetics, and close monitoring of electrolytes and blood pressure. A urinary catheter was placed due to acute retention, with resolution within 48 hours. The GI team evaluated her for possible outpatient EGD with Botox injection for gastroparesis. She gradually advanced to a regular diet, remained stable on subcutaneous insulin, and was discharged home with no medication changes and follow-up arranged with her GI physician.
